title: The summer Lake Washington fell
teaches: The 1916 lowering, the vanished Black River, and the locks that keep the salt out
summary: **A lake's level is set by its outlet.** The water rises until it spills over the lowest point of its rim, and settles a little above that lip.
**Lake Washington once drained south.** Before 1916 it spilled into the Black River at Renton, which joined the White River to form the Duwamish.
**The Cedar was turned into the lake in 1912.** Before that it joined the Black River below the lake.
**The Montlake Cut gave the lake a lower outlet.** When the cut opened in 1916 the lake drained west into Lake Union and fell about 2.7 metres (8.8 feet) over about two months.
**The Black River dried up.** The lake fell below its bed, so the river was left with only the rain from its own small valley.
**The locks at Ballard now set the lake's level.** Since 1917 the Hiram M. Chittenden Locks have held Lake Union and Lake Washington about 6 metres above low tide in the Sound.
**Every lockage lets salt water in.** Heavy sea water slides upstream along the bottom of Salmon Bay as a salt wedge.
**A barrier and a drain keep the salt from the lake.** A barrier on the lock chamber's floor holds salt water back, and a drain upstream returns what gets past to the Sound.

blocks.text: In the autumn of 1916, people along the south end of Lake Washington watched their lake go away. At Rainier Beach, on the southwest shore, docks built out into deep enough water for a launch ended over mud, and boathouses sat on the ground. Week by week the shoreline crept outward. At Renton, the Black River, which had carried the lake's water south for as long as anyone there remembered, ran thinner, and then stopped.

Nobody had dammed the Black River, and the summer had not been unusually dry. What had changed was some 15 km away, at the far north end of the lake, where workmen had just finished cutting a channel through a low neck of land into Lake Union. Lesson 6 looked at what goes on inside a lake. This lesson is about what holds one up. Before reading on, try to explain how a ditch dug at one end of a lake can dry up a river at the other.

parts.title: A lake with one way out

blocks.text: A lake is a hollow that has filled until it spills. The water rises until it reaches the lowest point on the hollow's rim, the lip, and pours over it as the lake's outlet river. The higher the water stands above the lip, the faster it pours, and the faster it pours the more steeply it grows with each extra centimetre, so a lake settles only a little above its lip: just high enough that the outflow matches what flows in.[^lip] In a wet winter the lake rides a little higher and in late summer a little lower. The lip decides the level.

Before 1916, Lake Washington's lip was at its south end. The lake spilled into the Black River, a short, slow river that wound southwest from Renton and joined the White River near present-day Tukwila; together they became the Duwamish, which ran on to Elliott Bay. The Cedar River did not then flow into the lake at all. It came down through Renton and joined the Black River just below the lake. In 1912, to ease Renton's floods and to give the planned canal more water, the Cedar was turned north into a new channel straight into the lake.

West of the lake, across the narrow neck of land at Montlake, lay Lake Union, some 2.7 metres lower, draining west through Salmon Bay to the Sound. People had talked of joining the lakes to the Sound since the 1850s, when the lake got its name for just that hope.[^union] The plan that was finally built had two parts: a cut through the Montlake neck, and locks at Ballard to hold the lakes up above the tide and lift ships into them.

blocks.caption: Lake Washington and its outlets from 1911 to 1917. The rivers and canals are drawn roughly; the shading shows today's lakes and shore, not the old ones.

stages.text: The lake spills south into the Black River. The Cedar joins the Black below the lake, and the Black joins the White near Tukwila to make the Duwamish.
The Cedar is turned north into a new channel and runs straight into the lake. The Black River now carries only the lake's own outflow.
The Montlake Cut opens. The lake drains west into Lake Union and falls about 2.7 m over about two months; the Black River runs dry.
The locks at Ballard open. The ship canal runs from Lake Washington through Lake Union and Salmon Bay to the Sound, and the locks hold the lakes about 6 m above low tide.

blocks.text: The Montlake Cut was dug dry, with a temporary dam, a cofferdam, left in place at its east end to hold Lake Washington back.[^cofferdam] In late August 1916 the cofferdam was opened and the lake began to pour west into Lake Union, through the cut and over the floor dug for it, far below the Black River's bed. From that day the lake had a new lip, and it was 2.7 metres lower.

blocks.caption: A model of the lake and its two outlets, south (left) to north and west (right), heights above low tide in the Sound. The inflow is a late summer's, and the cut's flow is set so the lake falls over about two months, as it did.
blocks.task: Guess, then run the days until the Black River stops

blocks.text: Once the lake fell below the Black River's bed, all its outflow went north, and the Black River had nothing left but the rain from its own small valley. Move the locks' level in the model and the reason shows: as long as the new outlet holds the water below the old lip, the old river is dead, and only if the locks held Lake Union above the Black River's bed would it run again.

**An estimate.** A fall of 2.7 m over the lake's 88 km² lets out about 0.24 km³ of water, roughly what the Cedar brings down in five months of average flow. Spread over two months, that is something like 40 m³ a second through the cut on top of the lake's ordinary outflow: a big river's worth, running through a ditch that had been dry ground a few years before.

parts.title: What the lake lost and gained

blocks.text: A drop of 2.7 metres around a lake with gently sloping shores uncovers a lot of ground. Marshes grew where shallow bays had been, at Union Bay below the University of Washington and at the mouth of Mercer Slough near Bellevue. Docks had to be lengthened all round the lake, and at Renton the Cedar's delta stood above water; much of it now lies under the city's airport.

The Duwamish people, whose villages stood along these rivers, lost the Black River and the fish that ran up it. The Duwamish River lost the lake's water as well. Lesson S3 follows what happened to it.

The locks at Ballard, named in 1956 for Hiram M. Chittenden, the Army engineer who planned them, were formally opened on 4 July 1917. Since then they, not any natural lip, have set the level of Lake Union and Lake Washington: about 6 metres above low tide in the Sound, let down a little each autumn to make room for winter rain and raised again in spring.[^datum] A boat going up waits in a chamber at the Sound's level while fresh water from above fills it, and rises with it by anything from about 2 metres at a high tide to about 8 at a very low one.

Each time a boat goes through, the Sound gets a way in. The chamber holds sea water when its lower gates open, and when the upper gates open, that heavy salt water slumps out along the bottom into Salmon Bay. Lesson 12 showed what salt water does where it meets a river: being heavier, it slides in underneath as a [[salt wedge|salt]] and stays there unless something stirs it. Left alone, it would creep along the floor of the ship canal into Lake Union, and then into Lake Washington, where it would sit on the bottom and, as lesson 6 explained, a heavy bottom layer stops the lake from mixing in winter.

blocks.caption: The large lock in section, with a boat just lifted: salt water (dark) left on the chamber's floor and creeping up Salmon Bay along the bottom, the barrier that holds it back, and the drain that sends it back to the Sound. Not to scale.

blocks.text: Two works keep it out. On the floor of the large lock, near its upstream gates, is a barrier that can be raised to hold back the bottom layer of salt water when the gates open. A little upstream, an intake on the bed of Salmon Bay catches the salt water that gets past and drains it back below the locks. Even so, a thin layer of salt water reaches some way up the canal in late summer, when the lake has little fresh water to spare.

**Go and look.** The locks are open to walk across most of the day. Stand by the large lock as it fills and watch the boats rise; look up the day's tide first, since the lift is largest at a low tide. On the south side, the fish ladder's windows show salmon heading upstream from July to September.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the lowered lake
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What sets the level of a natural lake?
choices: The lowest point of its rim, where it spills out: the lake settles a little above that lip
The amount of rain that falls on it, since the lake rises in step with each wet year
The depth of its deepest point, which holds a fixed volume of water below the surface
The height of the groundwater in the hills around it, which holds the water in like a wall
items.why: A lake fills until it spills, and the outflow grows quickly as the water rises above the lip, so the level stays close to the lip.

items.ask: Before 1916, which way did Lake Washington drain?
choices: South, through the Black River at Renton to the Duwamish
West, through Lake Union and Salmon Bay to the Sound
North, through the Sammamish River toward the Snohomish
Nowhere on the surface; its water left only through the ground
items.why: The Black River was the lake's outlet until the Montlake Cut gave it a lower one in 1916.

items.ask: Why did the Black River dry up in 1916, when no one dammed it?
choices: The lake fell below the river's bed once the cut gave it a lower outlet, so no lake water reached the river
The Cedar River was turned away from it that summer, taking away the river's main source of water
A dry summer lowered the water table under Renton, and the river's water sank into the ground
The locks at Ballard pumped water out of the lake to fill Lake Union for ships
items.why: With a new lip 2.7 m lower, the lake drained west and fell below the old one. The Cedar had been turned into the lake four years earlier.

items.ask: About how far did Lake Washington fall when the Montlake Cut opened?
choices: About 2.7 metres (8.8 feet), over about two months
About 30 centimetres (one foot), over a few days
About 9 metres (30 feet), over about a year
About 2.7 metres (8.8 feet), in a single night
items.why: The lake fell to the level of Lake Union, about 2.7 m lower, between late August and October 1916.

items.ask: Why does salt water get into Salmon Bay above the locks?
choices: Each lockage leaves sea water in the chamber, and being heavier it slides out along the bottom when the upper gates open
High tides in the Sound rise above the lake's level and spill over the top of the spillway dam
Salt seeps through the concrete walls of the locks from the Sound side all the time
Rain washes salt from the city's roads into the canal, and it gathers in the bay
items.why: The chamber fills with sea water at the Sound's level; that dense water creeps upstream along the floor as a salt wedge.

items.ask: Why does it matter if a salt layer reaches the bottom of Lake Washington?
choices: A heavy salty bottom layer would not mix with the water above it, even in winter, so the deep water would be cut off
The salt would make the whole lake too salty to drink within a few years of lockages
Salt water freezes at a higher temperature, so the lake would freeze over every winter
The salt would dissolve the lake's bed and deepen it until the shoreline moved back
items.why: Lake Washington mixes top to bottom once a winter; a denser salty layer on the floor would stay put and stop that mixing.

lip.title: Over the lip
lip.text: Water pouring over a broad lip flows faster the deeper it is, and the flow goes roughly as the depth over the lip to the power one and a half. Double the depth over the lip and the outflow nearly triples, which is why a lake's level swings much less than its inflow.

union.title: Lake Union
union.text: The settler Thomas Mercer is said to have named Lake Union at a Fourth of July picnic in 1854, for the union of waters he expected a canal to bring. A small log canal was cut at Montlake in the 1880s, but ships waited until the 1910s.

cofferdam.title: Cofferdam
cofferdam.text: A cofferdam is a temporary wall that keeps water out of a place being dug or built, then is removed.

datum.title: Measured from low tide
datum.text: Heights at the locks are measured from a datum close to the average of the lower low tides in the Sound. On that scale Lake Washington is held between about 20 feet in winter and about 22 feet in summer, or about 6.1 and 6.7 metres.
